subject: 25A32FCFEDFE4DDF82D196BFF21A9DFC
introduction: Consultation, in these readings, is both a law and an art: every matter great or small is to be settled by taking counsel together; each person offers a view as a contribution and lets it go; the clash of opinions brings out the spark of truth; and once a decision is reached, all act on it, the minority included. Many of the readings are brief replies to people who had asked what to do and were told to consult. Proverbs, Jethro's advice to Moses, the council at Jerusalem and the Qur’an's verse of counsel stand beside them, with Aristotle on the wisdom of the many and Bacon on the trust of counsel. Contrasts come from those who feared for the lone voice and the private judgment: Emerson, Descartes, Kant, Thoreau and Mill.
questions: What must a person give up, and what must a person bring, to consult in the way these readings describe?
The readings ask the minority to yield and, in a meeting, to keep quiet when they do not accept a decision. What do Mill and Thoreau fear in that, and what do the readings fear in the alternative?
Aristotle says the many together may judge better than the best few; Plato wanted philosophers as kings. Which do the readings side with, and on what condition?
One reading calls the outcome of consultation the command of God. How can that be held together with the admission that a decision may be mistaken?
Which matters in your own life would be different if they had been taken to consultation?

outside.why: Paul asks that nothing be done through strife or vainglory, each esteeming the other better than himself.
Proverbs gives the reading's figure of opinions that strike a spark: iron sharpens iron.
Emerson says, trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. What does it cost a person to offer a view as a contribution and not as right?
James asks every man to be swift to hear, slow to speak and slow to wrath.
Saxe's blind men, each sure of the part of the elephant he has touched, are each partly right and all wrong.
Proverbs says the way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but he that hearkens unto counsel is wise.
Milton trusts that truth is not put to the worse in a free and open encounter.
James tells anyone who lacks wisdom to ask of God, who gives to all liberally.
The Qur’an praises those whose affairs are a matter of counsel among them.
Proverbs says that where no counsel is the people fall, but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Bacon calls the giving of counsel the greatest trust between man and man, for to counsellors men commit the whole.
Proverbs says that every purpose is established by counsel, and that good advice should go before any contest.
Proverbs says that without counsel purposes are disappointed, but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
The Qur’an tells Muhammad to be lenient with his companions, to pardon them and consult with them upon the conduct of affairs.
Proverbs likens the sweetness of a friend's hearty counsel to ointment and perfume that rejoice the heart.
Jesus promises to be in the midst where two or three are gathered together in his name.
Acts remembers the first believers as of one heart and of one soul.
The psalm exclaims how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Paul asks the Philippians to be likeminded, having the same love and being of one accord.
Aristotle wants unity in a state only in some respects, lest harmony pass into unison. Is being at one in body and soul what deliberation needs, or what it risks?
Aristotle grants that the many, meeting together, may be better than the few best, as a feast to which many contribute is better than one man's dinner.
Descartes resolved never to accept anything as true that he did not himself clearly know to be so. Is the counsel of several always weightier than one mind working alone?
Jethro tells Moses that judging alone is too heavy for him: thou art not able to perform it thyself alone.
The Preacher says two are better than one, for they have a good reward for their labour.
The Qur’an warns that conjecture can by no means take the place of truth.
The Buddha says of those who quarrel over views that they are people seeing one side.
Acts records that the apostles and elders came together to consider a disputed matter.
Jesus asks who would build a tower without first sitting down and counting the cost.
Told that Chi Wan thought thrice before acting, Confucius said that twice may do. When does deliberation over several days become delay?
Proverbs says: hear counsel and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end.
The council at Jerusalem sends its decision with the words, it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.
Mill held that mankind would not be justified in silencing one dissenter. What becomes of the four when the five have decided?
A hymn of the Rig Veda bids the assembly speak together with minds of one accord.
Proverbs says a wise man will hear and increase learning, and attain unto wise counsels.
The Laws tell Socrates that a citizen must do what his city orders, or else persuade it of what is just.
Thoreau asks why every man has a conscience if he must resign it to the legislator. Is submission to an assembly's decision ever a surrender of conscience?
Proverbs observes that a soft answer turns away wrath, while grievous words stir up anger.
Paul asks that speech be good for edifying, that it may minister grace to the hearers.
Proverbs says that he who has knowledge spares his words, a rule for the one who disagrees.
Mill warns that what is not fully and fearlessly discussed becomes a dead dogma. What does a meeting gain, and what does it lose, when the one who disagrees keeps quiet?
The apostles ask the disciples to look out among them seven men of honest report, full of wisdom.
Solomon asks for an understanding heart to judge, that he may discern between good and bad.
Tennyson imagined a parliament of man in which the affairs of all are referred to one gathering.
Paul finds that in the assembly every one has a psalm, a doctrine, a revelation, and asks that all be done unto edifying.
Jefferson reminds a divided assembly that every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle.
Hebrews asks believers not to forsake assembling together, but to stir one another up to love and good works.
Tocqueville saw Americans of every condition constantly forming associations to conduct their common affairs.
Acts says that at Pentecost they were all with one accord in one place.
Pericles says that ordinary citizens, though busy with industry, are still fair judges of public matters.
Amos asks the question that fits a household too: can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Paul wants the members of one body to have the same care one for another.
Paul asks believers to bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Proverbs asks that a child be trained up in the way he should go.
Jesus says that he who is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.
Paul beseeches a divided church to be perfectly joined together in the same mind and judgment.
Proverbs says that the memory of the just is blessed, a reason to leave some trace of a name.
Jesus says the harvest truly is plenteous but the labourers are few, and asks for more.
Isaiah hears the question, whom shall I send, and answers, here am I; send me.
The Qur’an tells believers to call unto the way of their Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation.
Zechariah asks, of a small beginning, who has despised the day of small things.
Proverbs says that a word spoken in due season, how good is it.
Proverbs notes that the first to plead his cause seems just, until another comes and searches him.
Confucius holds that learning without thought is labour lost, and thought without learning perilous.
Proverbs counsels trust in the Lord and not leaning on one's own understanding.
Bacon advises reading not to contradict nor to take for granted, but to weigh and consider.
Kant's motto was to have courage to use your own reason without direction from another. Is consulting on every matter, great and small, a help to judgment or a way of not forming one?
Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men and consulted the young men who had grown up with him.
Aristotle holds that he who bids the law rule bids God and reason rule.
Locke holds that reason must be our last judge and guide in every thing. What, if anything, stands above the outcome of consultation?
Proverbs says that faithful are the wounds of a friend, whose advice may be unwelcome and sound.
Proverbs says a talebearer reveals secrets, but one of a faithful spirit conceals the matter.
The Preacher says: be not rash with thy mouth, and let thy words be few.
Jesus sends his disciples out to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.
Paul asks that speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, fitted to each hearer.
Peter asks believers to be all of one mind, pitiful and courteous.
Jesus asks that a difference be taken first to the brother himself, between thee and him alone.
Isaiah has God himself say, come now, and let us reason together, an invitation and not a decree.
Jesus says that if two shall agree on earth about anything they ask, it shall be done for them.
The first psalm blesses the man who walks not in the counsel of the ungodly.
Mill warns that he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that. What is missed when counsel is taken only with those of like assurance?
Locke thought nine parts of ten of what men are, good or evil, comes by their education.
James says that as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.
Jesus likens whoever hears and does to a man who built his house upon a rock.
Portia says that if to do were as easy as to know what were good to do, chapels had been churches.
Roosevelt gives the credit to the one who actually strives to do the deeds, and errs, and tries again.
Paul's rule is to prove all things and hold fast that which is good.
Aesop's father shows his sons that sticks bound together cannot be broken: union gives strength.
Paul asks believers not to be weary in well doing, for in due season they shall reap.
Joshua is told to be strong and of a good courage, for the Lord is with him wherever he goes.
Carlyle held that conviction is worthless till it convert itself into conduct.
Confucius calls it knowledge to hold what you know and allow what you do not know.
Paul asks each not to think of himself more highly than he ought, but soberly.
James says that every kind of beast has been tamed, but the tongue can no man tame.
Milton welcomed much arguing and many opinions as knowledge in the making. Where should limits fall if the freedom of speech is both to be extolled and feared?
Jesus tells his disciples not to be called Rabbi or master, for all ye are brethren.
Plato held that cities will have no rest from evils until philosophers are kings. Is the judgment of the wise worth less than the consultation of the many?
Paul asks believers to forbear one another in love and keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
The apostles tell a council that they ought to obey God rather than men. How can the outcome of a consultation be called the command of God and still be open to correction?
Paul says the body is one and has many members, and no member can say it has no need of another.
Jesus pictures a king who sits down first and consults whether he is able before he acts.

proverbs-hearkeneth-unto-counsel.text: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise

proverbs-purpose-established-by-counsel.text: Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war

proverbs-hear-counsel-and-receive-instru.text: Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end

acts-came-together-to-consider.text: And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter

kings-forsook-the-counsel-of-the-old-men.text: But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him, and which stood before him

aristotle-feast-to-which-many-contribute.text: For the many, of whom each individual is but an ordinary person, when they meet together may very likely be better than the few good, if regarded not individually but collectively, just as a feast to which many contribute is better than a dinner provided out of a single purse
aristotle-feast-to-which-many-contribute.author: Aristotle

bacon-trust-of-giving-counsel.text: The greatest trust between man and man is the trust of giving counsel; for in other confidences men commit the parts of life, their lands, their goods, their children, their credit, some particular affair; but to such as they make their counsellors they commit the whole
bacon-trust-of-giving-counsel.author: Francis Bacon
